steps.explain: Leave a small gap between lanes, smaller when there are many cores so the lanes don't get too thin.
Take the gaps out of the area's height, then share what's left equally: that's each lane's height.
One rectangle per core, stacked top to bottom: lane `i` starts `i` lanes (and gaps) below the top. Every lane is as wide as the area.
Start with no moves.
For each program, find which core it was on last tick (`null` if none) and compare with the core it's on now. A different core means the scheduler moved it: onto a core, off one, or across.
Programs that stayed where they were don't show up at all.
Raised: every `irq` message on the bus this tick is a device asking for attention. Its address is the handler (the vector) it wants.
Was this core already running a handler last tick? (No previous tick: no.)
Taken: a core that's in a handler now but wasn't last tick has just started one. Its PC tells us which handler.
The board shows both: raised first, then taken.
One lane per core, leaving room for the title above and the notes line below.
What changed since last tick: the scheduler's moves (none on the very first tick) and the interrupt markers.
Turn the moves, the markers and the interrupts still waiting into short sentences for the notes line.
Draw the title, each core in its own lane in its own colour, and the notes line (red when something happened this tick).

timer-input.code:
if (input.action === "start") return { ...state, fsm: timerFsm.go(state.fsm, "COUNTING") };
return { ...state, fsm: timerFsm.go(state.fsm, "STOPPED"), elapsed: 0 };

steps.explain: Start: move the timer's state machine to `COUNTING`. It keeps the ticks counted so far.
Anything else is stop: go to `STOPPED` and forget the ticks counted, so the next start waits a full interval.
A stopped timer does nothing on a tick.
Count this tick. Not a full interval yet: just remember the count.
A full interval: start counting again from 0, note one more firing, and raise one `irq`.

Only between instructions: `IDLE` (nothing to run) or `FETCH` (the last instruction finished, the next hasn't started). Mid-`LOAD` the core is waiting for memory and can't be interrupted. And never while it's already running a handler: one interrupt at a time.
Taking an interrupt at the wrong moment is a bug in the caller, so stop loudly.
Remember where to come back to: idle again, or the next instruction.
The frame: everything `IRET` needs to put the program back exactly as it was. The flags matter: without them a `JNZ` after the handler could jump the wrong way.
Push the frame, jump to the handler (the vector), and fetch its first instruction.
The frame saved when the interrupt was taken. None means `IRET` ran outside a handler: that's a fault.
Put everything back: the phase it was in, its registers, PC, flags and instruction count, and empty the stack. The program carries on as if nothing happened.
